items.title: Female crash-test dummies
items.claim: Standard crash-test dummies are based on male physiology. When was a regulated female-sized dummy widely required in US tests?

options.text: Female-sized dummies were not required in US frontal crash tests until 2003 and a fully biofidelic female dummy is still under development

items.reveal_title: Required test dummies under-represented women for decades
items.reveal:
Caroline Criado Perez (Invisible Women, 2019) and NHTSA documents show female-sized dummies only became required in some US frontal tests from 2003, and a more biofidelic THOR-AV female dummy is still being developed.

Women face higher serious-injury risk in comparable crashes.
items.why: Standardised testing reflects the assumptions of its designers and reshapes downstream safety for those left out.

items.title: The Phoebus cartel
items.claim: In 1924 major light bulb manufacturers met in Geneva and agreed to limit bulb lifetimes. From what figure to what?
items.reveal:
The Phoebus cartel (Osram, Philips, GE and others) coordinated lower lifetime targets and tested members' compliance.

The cartel dissolved by 1939 but the case remains a foundational example of planned obsolescence in design history.
items.why: Designed lifespans are choices, not inevitabilities of materials or physics.

items.title: Morris's contradiction
items.claim: William Morris's Arts and Crafts movement (founded 1860s) argued for handmade goods accessible to all. What was the tension critics identified?

options.text: Handmade goods proved expensive, reaching mostly affluent buyers

items.reveal:
Morris & Co. produced wallpaper, textiles and furniture at prices that mostly the prosperous middle classes could afford. Morris himself recognised the contradiction.

The movement nonetheless reshaped expectations of designed everyday objects.
items.why: Design movements often struggle with the economics of their own ideals.
